addedResources.name: Unicode Standard Annex #15: Unicode Normalization Forms
addedResources.use: Read Sections 1.1 and 1.2: canonical versus compatibility equivalence, the four forms NFD, NFC, NFKD and NFKC, and why the compatibility forms can remove distinctions that matter. Use it to decide which form belongs to a matching key and which, if any, to stored text.

units.title: Corpus purpose, target population, provenance and usage rights
outcomes: Write a corpus purpose statement that names the intended model behaviour and the population of text and users it must serve, and state what the corpus must not be used for.
Trace one source from live site to crawl to dump to your files, and record at each hop the licence or consent basis, the restrictions that apply and what is still unknown.
Explain why a stable source and document id, kept through every later version, is what makes a deletion or blocklist request actionable.
units.why: Every filter and mixture choice later in this section is judged against what the corpus is for, and every rights question is answered from a record made when the data was acquired. A record you did not keep at download time cannot be rebuilt afterwards.

next.note: Carry the source and record identity you define here through extraction.
Turn the ledger into the sources and rights sections of a data card.

study.title: Dolma Toolkit: data format
study.locator: 'Dolma Document Format' with the `id` field and the `metadata` field

focus: State the purpose before you filter: the behaviour the model must have and the population it serves. Dolma scopes itself to English text on purpose and says that this reinforces English as the default (Section 3), which is what makes its English-only rules defensible.

A page reaches you through several hops, and each hop has its own rules: `robots.txt` and terms of service at crawl time, copyright and any licence on the content, and the licence on the collection that redistributes it. Keep one row per source and mark each field verified, assumed or unknown.

A collection licence does not pass to the documents inside it, and a content licence does not override a site's terms of service. The lecture's CommonPile list and the YouTube example make both points.

A deletion or takedown request can be honoured only if the document id is stable across every later version and every derived artifact keeps it. Dolma requires this of the `id` field so that a blocklist applies to all versions.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the one-page ledger for a corpus you plan to build: a purpose statement of three or four lines (behaviour, population, out-of-scope uses), then one row per source with `source`, `acquired_from`, `date`, `basis` (licence, consent or exception claimed), `restrictions` (`robots.txt`, terms), `personal_data`, `deletion_contact` and `unknown`. Mark every cell verified, assumed or unknown, and list which cells you could not fill from the data alone.
traps: Treating 'it is in the crawl' as 'it may be used for training'. A crawl records how you obtained a page, not what its owner permits.

Writing the purpose as a list of sources ('web, code, books'). That gives you nothing to test filters against: Dodge Sections 5.2 and 5.3 show a blocklist removing text by and about minority groups, which counts as a loss only if those groups are in the population you stated.
Filling the rights record after the download. The date, the version of the terms and the `robots.txt` you saw at that time cannot be rebuilt later, so capture them while acquiring.

selfTest.q: A page is in the crawl snapshot you downloaded. Give two separate reasons you may still be unable to train on it.
selfTest.a: The owner holds copyright unless a licence or an exception such as fair use applies, and that exception is unsettled. Independently, the site's terms of service or `robots.txt` can restrict automated copying even when the content is licensed, and the page may contain personal data.

selfTest.q: Why must a document id stay the same from the raw files to every later dataset version?
selfTest.a: A blocklist for takedown requests, evaluation leaks or manual rejection is a list of ids. If ids were reassigned per version, the list would stop matching the later versions without any error, and a deleted document could survive in them.

selfTest.q: A corpus is released under a permissive collection licence. Can you assume each document in it is free to use?
selfTest.a: No. The collection licence covers the compilation. Each document keeps whatever status its owner gave it, so you still need a per-source basis, and laundering of copyrighted work into a permissive collection is a known risk.

selfTest.q: A corpus is scoped to English on purpose. Name one thing that scope justifies and one claim it does not support.
selfTest.a: It justifies English-specific rules such as a stop-word test or an English language-ID threshold. It does not support any claim about how a model trained on it behaves in other languages, and the scope should be stated in the card so readers do not infer one.

units.title: WARC and HTML text extraction with document boundaries preserved
outcomes: Implement text extraction from raw HTML bytes that tries UTF-8 first, falls back to a detected encoding, and records which route it took.
Iterate the response records of a WARC file so that each record yields exactly one document that keeps its record id, URL and date.
Compare full-page and main-content extraction on pages you have read, and say what each one removes, keeps and cannot recover.
units.why: Extraction decides what text exists at all. Navigation text left in becomes repeated text that every later step must catch, and a document that loses its record id can no longer be traced to a source or deleted.

next.note: Score each extracted document for language and decide what text cleaning you can undo.
Boilerplate that survives extraction is the first thing deduplication has to find.

study.locator: Section 2.2, HTML to text conversion, and Problem (`extract_text`) parts (a) and (b) (pp. 3 to 4), with the FastWARC note

study.title: FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024)
study.locator: arXiv:2406.17557v2, Section 3.1 (experimental setup, for how each choice is ablated) and Section 3.2 (text extraction: WARC versus WET, Figure 1)
study.depth: Stop after Section 3.2 here; Sections 3.3 and 3.4 belong to the filtering and deduplication units.

study.title: Resiliparse: HTML2Text and FastWARC
study.locator: HTML2Text sections 'Basic Plain Text Conversion' and 'Main Content Extraction'; then the FastWARC page at https://resiliparse.chatnoir.eu/en/stable/man/fastwarc.html, sections 'Iterating WARC Files', 'Filtering Records', 'Record Properties' and 'Freezing Records' (page read 2026-10-16, Resiliparse and FastWARC 1.0.9)

focus: A WARC file interleaves record types. Only `response` records hold a page; `request`, `warcinfo` and `metadata` records are not documents. Select the type when you open the iterator.

The document identity comes from the WARC header: `record_id` is the `WARC-Record-ID`, and the target URI and date sit beside it. Write them next to the text at the moment you extract, because nothing later can recover them.

Extraction is lossy and a choice, not a fact. With `main_content=False` (the default) `extract_plain_text` keeps navigation and footer text; with `main_content=True` it removes them, and it can also remove short real text such as list items and captions. FineWeb found WET text retained too much menu text and that extraction changed the trained model.
Bytes come first. Try UTF-8, fall back to `detect_encoding`, and keep the encoding you used in the record, since a wrong guess produces plausible but damaged text.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write `extract_records(warc_path)` that opens the file with FastWARC, keeps only `response` records, decodes the body (UTF-8 first, then the detected encoding), calls `extract_plain_text`, and yields a dict with `record_id`, `url`, `date`, `encoding` and `text`. On a WARC you build with three response records and one request record, show that you get three documents and that `record_id` matches the header. Then run one page with `main_content=False` and `True` and write down one piece of text the second setting removed correctly and, if you can find one, one it removed wrongly.
traps: Passing the course test and believing boilerplate is gone. The fixture's expected text equals the default output (`main_content=False`), and with `main_content=True` it no longer matches, so the test checks decoding and plain-text conversion, not boilerplate removal. Measure that separately on pages you read.
Reading `record.reader.read()` twice. The reader is a live stream, so the second call returns empty bytes; call `freeze()` first if you need the payload again.

Storing documents as one text file and treating each line as a document. Extracted pages contain newlines, so the handout's tokenization starter, which adds the end-of-text token after every line, would insert document boundaries inside documents. Store one JSON object per document and tokenize each document as a unit.

selfTest.q: A WARC file has 10 records: 1 `warcinfo`, 4 `request` and 5 `response`. How many documents should extraction produce, and where does each one's id come from?
selfTest.a: Five, one per response record. The id is the `WARC-Record-ID` header of that record, read as `record_id` in FastWARC.

selfTest.q: Why can the same HTML give different training text under `main_content=True` and `main_content=False`, and which output is the better training data?
selfTest.a: The default keeps navigation, footer and sign-in text, and the main-content setting removes it and can also remove short real text such as a list item. Neither is better in general: it depends on what the page is and on what the model is for, so decide by reading samples and by an ablation, as FineWeb did, not by assumption.

selfTest.q: A page declares no charset and its bytes are Latin-1 text. What happens if you decode it as UTF-8 with `errors='replace'`, and what should the pipeline do instead?
selfTest.a: Bytes above 127 usually fail as UTF-8 and become replacement characters, so accented letters are lost silently. Fall back to a detected encoding, keep the encoding you used in the record, and count how often the fallback runs.

selfTest.q: Why is it a boundary bug to concatenate extracted documents into one file separated by blank lines?
selfTest.a: A blank line also occurs inside documents, so the original document boundaries cannot be recovered. Use an explicit record format with the id, or an end-of-document marker that cannot occur in the text, and test that the document count survives a write and read.

units.title: Language and domain identification, and irreversible normalization decisions
outcomes: Implement language identification with fastText that returns a language and a score between 0 and 1, and choose a keep threshold from a hand-labelled sample with a stated interval, not from the score alone.
Measure retention per language and per kind of text at a threshold, and find which languages, short texts, code and mixed pages the filter drops or mislabels.
Choose a Unicode normalization form for each stage, state which distinctions it erases, and keep the raw text so that the choice can be revisited.
units.why: A language filter decides which languages the model will ever see, and a normalization step decides which character distinctions it can ever learn. Both are applied once, at scale, and a bad choice cannot be undone from the cleaned output.

next.note: Rule-based quality filters assume a language; check what they do outside English.
The languages you keep set the languages your tokenizer must handle.

study.title: FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024)
study.locator: arXiv:2406.17557v2, Section 3.3 (base filtering: a fastText English score of at least 0.65)
study.depth: Read only the language-filter sentence; the rest of 3.3 belongs to the quality-filter unit.

focus: The off-the-shelf identifier, `lid.176.bin`, returns a label and a probability for text on one line; it was trained on Wikipedia, Tatoeba and SETimes, and it knows 176 languages. A text in any other language still gets one of those labels.

A threshold such as 0.5 or 0.65 is a pipeline policy, not a property of the model. The score is not calibrated across languages, so measure retention per language on parallel or hand-labelled text before you fix the number.
Sample and audit: read labelled examples, count errors per slice, and report the error rate with an interval. Twenty samples can only bound an error rate loosely.

Normalization has two kinds of use. A matching key (for deduplication or contamination) may be aggressive because you keep the original. Stored training text should change only distinctions the standard says carry no meaning. NFKC does not meet that bar, which is Gopher's own conclusion.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write `identify(text)` that removes newlines, calls `predict(text, k=1)` on `lid.176.bin`, and returns `(code, score)`. Run it on the 1,012 `devtest` sentences of FLORES-200 (CC BY-SA 4.0) for English, Swahili, Yoruba and Shan, and tabulate top-1 accuracy, the share of sentences that are both correct and at least 0.65, and the mean score. In one run with fastText 0.9.2 (the `fasttext-numpy2-wheel` build) and `lid.176.bin`, English was 100% correct with 99.7% kept, Swahili 94.8% correct but only 28.7% kept, Yoruba 56.0% correct with 200 sentences labelled Irish, and every Shan sentence but one was labelled Burmese (mean score 0.89, since Shan is not among the 176). Then write what NFC and NFKC each do to `ﬁ` (U+FB01), the full-width `Ｈｅｌｌｏ` and `x²`, and say which result you could not undo.
traps: Reading the score as a probability of being right. Shan was labelled Burmese at a mean score of 0.89, and a short Norwegian Bokmål sentence (`Jeg bor i en liten by ved kysten og går til jobb hver dag.`) came back Danish at 0.96 in the same setup. A high score says the model is sure, not that it is correct.
Using one threshold for every language. A cutoff that keeps 99.7% of English can keep under a third of correctly identified Swahili, so a global rule silently removes a language from the corpus.

Cleaning the stored text with the same normalization you use for dedup keys. Lowercasing, accent stripping and whitespace collapse (the handout's MinHash step) are fine for a key; applied to the training text they erase case, diacritics and the indentation in code.

selfTest.q: A model is right on 94.8% of Swahili sentences, yet an English-tuned cutoff of 0.65 keeps 28.7% of them. What does this tell you about choosing a threshold?
selfTest.a: The score distribution differs by language, so one number trades very different amounts of recall per language. Choose the cutoff per language, or per slice, from a labelled sample, and report retention by language.

selfTest.q: You audit 300 sampled documents and find no language errors. What can you claim about the error rate?
selfTest.a: Only an upper bound: with 0 errors in 300 the 95% upper bound is about 1.2% (Clopper-Pearson), roughly 3 divided by 300. You cannot claim zero, and the bound holds for the population you sampled from, not for slices you did not sample.

selfTest.q: Why can NFKC be used to build a deduplication key but should not be applied to the text you train on?
selfTest.a: NFKC replaces compatibility forms, for example `x²` becomes `x2` and ligatures and full-width letters become plain letters. A key only needs to treat such variants as equal, and the original stays available. Stored text would lose distinctions that math, code and typography rely on, and the change cannot be reversed from the output.

selfTest.q: A four-line Python function is labelled Swedish at 0.27. What does this say about running language identification on mixed web data?
selfTest.a: The identifier was trained on prose, so code, tables and markup get arbitrary labels and low scores. A language threshold would remove them as a side effect. Decide the domain first and route code and non-prose to their own rules.
